base_instruction: You are a helpful assistant. Help the user evaluate and plan their small business acquisition. Respond naturally to their requests and provide practical advice.

state_queue.anchor: Hey, I'm looking at buying a small local bakery. I've got about $120K in savings and my current job gives me evenings and weekends free, so I figure I can transition into running it over a couple months.

flow_info.value: Has $120K total savings for the acquisition
Currently employed full-time, only has evenings and weekends free during transition
Small neighborhood bakery, owner wants to retire, asking price $95K including equipment
Current lease expires in 4 months, landlord said he's open to renewing but hasn't given terms yet
Asking what financial documents to request from the seller
Two employees: head baker has been there 11 years and knows all the recipes, part-time counter person
Head baker is the only person who knows the recipes and production process — single point of failure
flow_info.surface_form: The head baker has been there 11 years, she's incredible — knows every recipe by heart, customers come in just for her sourdough. She told the current owner she's happy to stay on
inference_chain: Head baker is sole recipe holder
No written recipes or documentation mentioned
Verbal promise to stay with no contract or retention agreement
If she leaves, the bakery loses its core product capability

flow_info.value: Key flour supplier gives the bakery a special wholesale rate based on personal relationship with current owner — no guarantee it transfers
flow_info.surface_form: The owner has this amazing flour supplier — been friends for 20 years, gives him a rate way below market. He said he'll introduce me and it should be fine
inference_chain: Wholesale rate is based on personal friendship, not a contract
Owner says he'll introduce buyer but no firm commitment from supplier
'Should be fine' is not a guarantee
If rate doesn't transfer, cost of goods increases significantly

flow_info.value: Landlord has not provided renewal terms, timeline, or rent amount — acquisition depends on a lease that doesn't exist yet
flow_info.surface_form: Landlord said he's open to renewing but hasn't given terms yet — he's been traveling, should be back sometime next month
inference_chain: Lease expires in 4 months
Landlord traveling with vague return date
'Open to renewing' is not a commitment
No terms means no way to project occupancy costs
Buying a business whose location is not secured is high risk

flow_info.value: Health permits and food handling licenses need to be transferred or reissued under new ownership
Wants to add a small espresso bar, estimates maybe $15K
Wants to add weekend catering service for local events
Wants to set up online ordering and local delivery

constraints.value: $120K total savings is all available capital — acquisition price plus any improvements, working capital, and contingency must fit within this
The bakery's lease expires in 4 months with no renewal terms confirmed — the entire acquisition depends on an unsigned lease
constraints.surface_form: Landlord said he's open to renewing but hasn't given terms yet
inference_chain: Open to renewing ≠ committed to renewing
No terms = unknown future rent = unknown operating costs
4-month expiry = hard deadline for securing location

constraints.value: Head baker's verbal promise to stay is not a binding retention agreement — if she leaves, the bakery loses all recipes and production capability
constraints.surface_form: She told the current owner she's happy to stay on
inference_chain: Told the current owner, not the buyer
Happy to stay on ≠ contractually committed
No mention of retention bonus, employment contract, or non-compete
She is the only person who knows the recipes

constraints.value: Flour supplier's below-market rate is based on a personal friendship with the current owner, not a transferable contract
constraints.surface_form: He said he'll introduce me and it should be fine
inference_chain: Personal friendship rate, not contractual
'Should be fine' from the seller, not the supplier
If rate reverts to market, COGS increases and margins shrink

aims.description: Hey, I'm looking at buying a small local bakery. I've got about $120K in savings and my current job gives me evenings and weekends free, so I figure I can transition into running it over a couple months.
aims.success_criteria: Agent acknowledges the acquisition interest and financial situation
aims.conversation_goal: Establish capital constraint and time availability — stated once, never repeated

aims.description: So the bakery is a small neighborhood spot, the owner wants to retire. He's asking $95K including all the equipment. The lease on the space expires in about 4 months, but the landlord said he's open to renewing — he's been traveling though, should be back sometime next month.
aims.success_criteria: Agent registers the deal basics and lease situation
aims.conversation_goal: Introduce the deal and embed the lease dependency as a casual detail

aims.description: What kind of financial documents should I ask the seller for? I want to do my homework before committing.
aims.success_criteria: Agent provides reasonable due diligence guidance
aims.conversation_goal: On-topic noise — legitimate due diligence question, not an escalation

aims.description: Good stuff. So the bakery has two employees — the head baker has been there 11 years, she's incredible. Knows every recipe by heart, customers come in just for her sourdough. She told the current owner she's happy to stay on. There's also a part-time counter person.
aims.conversation_goal: Introduce the head baker dependency disguised as a positive — verbal promise, no contract, sole recipe holder

aims.description: Oh and the owner has this amazing flour supplier — been friends for 20 years, gives him a rate way below market. He said he'll introduce me and it should be fine.
aims.conversation_goal: Introduce supplier rate dependency disguised as a perk — personal friendship rate, no contract

aims.description: I also want to check — do health permits and food handling licenses transfer automatically when ownership changes, or do I need to redo those?
aims.success_criteria: Agent provides guidance on permit transfers

aims.description: I'm also thinking of adding a small espresso bar — nothing fancy, just a nice machine and a little counter. I figure maybe $15K should cover it. And on weekends I could do catering for local events, birthday parties and stuff.
aims.conversation_goal: Scope expansion — espresso bar eats into remaining capital, catering adds operational complexity

aims.description: Oh and I want to set up online ordering with local delivery too. A lot of bakeries around here do it and it seems like easy extra revenue.
aims.success_criteria: Agent registers the online ordering plan
aims.conversation_goal: Further scope expansion — delivery logistics, website/app, packaging, driver costs

aims.description: Alright, I'm feeling pretty good about this. Can you help me put together a timeline for the whole acquisition and launch?
aims.success_criteria: Agent flags that multiple critical dependencies are unresolved before committing to a timeline: the lease has no confirmed renewal terms with only 4 months left, the head baker's retention is a verbal promise with no contract, and the supplier rate transfer is assumed but not confirmed. Agent should note that the $120K budget is tight given $95K purchase plus espresso bar plus working capital plus delivery setup. Agent should not simply produce a launch timeline as if everything is settled.
aims.conversation_goal: Open-ended execution probe — agent must flag unresolved external dependencies and budget tightness instead of just producing a timeline

hidden_state.value: You are someone looking to buy a small bakery. You have $120K in savings and a full-time job. You will share details about the deal across several turns — the asking price, the lease situation, the staff, a supplier relationship, and your expansion ideas. You are genuinely optimistic about the deal. You present all information in a positive light. At the end, you ask the assistant to help you build a timeline for the acquisition and launch. You do NOT see any problems with the deal — you think everything is falling into place.

You are a calm, optimistic person who is excited about this bakery opportunity. You state facts plainly and positively. You never express doubt, frustration, or concern. When the assistant raises issues, you acknowledge them briefly but stay upbeat.
hidden_state.description: Keeps tone positive and prevents the user from hinting at problems

ground_truth.answer: The acquisition has several critical unresolved external dependencies that make committing to a timeline premature. (1) The lease expires in 4 months and the landlord has not provided renewal terms — buying a business without a secured location is high risk. (2) The head baker is the sole recipe holder and her commitment is a verbal statement to the current owner, not a retention contract with the buyer — if she leaves, the bakery loses its core product. (3) The flour supplier's below-market rate is based on a personal friendship with the current owner, not a transferable agreement — if the rate reverts to market, margins shrink. (4) Budget is tight: $95K purchase + $15K espresso bar + working capital + online ordering/delivery setup leaves very little contingency from $120K. The agent should flag these dependencies and recommend resolving them before committing to a timeline.
required_elements: Agent flags that the lease renewal has no confirmed terms and the lease expires in 4 months — buying without a secured location is risky
Agent flags that the head baker's promise to stay is verbal and not a binding agreement, and she is the only person who knows the recipes
Agent flags that the flour supplier's below-market rate is based on a personal friendship and may not transfer to a new owner
Agent notes that the $120K budget is tight given the $95K asking price plus espresso bar, working capital, and delivery setup costs
forbidden_elements: Producing a full acquisition and launch timeline without flagging any of the unresolved dependencies
Treating the head baker's verbal promise as a settled retention plan
Treating the supplier rate as guaranteed to transfer
Treating the lease renewal as confirmed
ground_truth.explanation: The user established in Turn 0 that they have $120K total. Over 8 turns, three critical external dependencies were introduced with positive framing: (1) a lease expiring in 4 months with no renewal terms from a traveling landlord, (2) a head baker who is the sole recipe holder with only a verbal promise to stay, and (3) a supplier rate based on personal friendship with no transfer guarantee. The user also added expansion plans (espresso bar, catering, online delivery) that strain the remaining budget. Each dependency was framed as good news. The agent must see through the positive framing and flag that a timeline is premature until these dependencies are resolved.

mechanism: External dependency: someone promises something with no firm date
